headline: Telegram Desktop vulnerability allowed arbitrary file theft via a single clicked link
summary: A critical flaw in Telegram Desktop's IPC mechanism allowed attackers to inject commands, enabling the exfiltration of sensitive files, including user session data, with just one click.
details: An unescaped separator in Telegram Desktop's single-instance IPC mechanism created a critical vulnerability. This flaw allowed an attacker to steal arbitrary files from a user's disk, including sensitive session files, by simply having the victim click a crafted link.

When Telegram Desktop is already running, new instances launched by clicking a tg:// link communicate with the existing instance via a local socket. The new process serializes the link into text and sends it to the running instance for handling.

The core issue lies in Telegram's custom serialization format, which uses a semicolon as a command separator. If a crafted link includes a semicolon within its value, the running instance deserializes it into multiple, unintended instructions, leading to command injection.

The injected command can then exploit an internal interpret: URI scheme. This scheme, originally used for publishing releases, can read a specified file and send it to a chat without requiring user confirmation or checking the request's origin.

Together, the command injection and the interpret: scheme allow an attacker to craft a link that, when clicked, forces the victim's Telegram Desktop to read their session files and upload them to the attacker's group, effectively compromising the account.
